content:
Amy Eskridge (1987–2022) was an American researcher from Huntsville, Alabama, USA. Her name has gained increasing prominence in discussions surrounding anti-gravity technology, advanced propulsion systems, UFOs/UAPs, and the alleged secrecy surrounding unconventional scientific research. She is also among a group of scientists and researchers associated with these fields who have reportedly died or disappeared under unusual circumstances in recent years. 


She made one of her most intriguing statements during a 2020 interview with Jeremy Rys and Mark Sokol, when she said: "They are from the future. They are from here. They are you, they are me." 

She referred to what are known as ultraterrestrials, beings believed to originate on Earth, who could potentially be descendants of an ancient form of humanity, rather than extraterrestrials originating from elsewhere in the universe. 

Eskridge explained two classifications: 

P-47: Present + 47,000 years. 

P-52: Present + 52,000 years. 

According to Amy, these beings would be descendants of present-day humanity, living tens of thousands of years in our future. 

If her statement were true, it would fundamentally change how we understand UFO phenomena. Suppose an advanced human civilization existed 50,000 years in our future. Could some UFO sightings represent technology developed by a future human civilization? 

Instead of asking whether extraterrestrials are visiting Earth from another solar system, we would have to consider whether some encounters might involve descendants of humanity itself.  

Interestingly, during an interview with late-night talk show host Stephen Colbert, Steven Spielberg suggested the possibility that the beings behind the UFO phenomenon might actually be us from the future. That is a fascinating hypothesis, especially when considered alongside the theories Amy Eskridge discussed about ultraterrestrials. Spielberg's access to influential people in Hollywood, government and scientific circles may have exposed him to unusual perspectives and information. 

It is quite possible that, during her research, Amy discovered something significant that provided a basis for her statements and theories. Unfortunately, she died on June 11, 2022, in Huntsville, Alabama. Her death was officially reported as a suicide by gunshot, although the circumstances surrounding her death continue to raise questions and remain a subject of controversy.
